title: Run a chip factory
summary: A 3D fab you run: why chips take months, why one machine group sets the pace, and who feeds it.

then: People carry open cassettes of {wafer} wafers from machine to machine in the cleanroom.
300 mm fabs: sealed boxes of 25 wafers ride robot cars on ceiling rails between the bays.
EUV scanners print the finest layers of phone chips in one pass instead of two.
High-NA EUV prints select layers in volume, and AI helps fabs schedule, inspect and maintain.

challenges.title: Wafers go round
challenges.task: Pick the AI chip and follow its box. How many times will it pass the scanners in the lithography bay?
challenges.hint: Look at the chip's layers in the cross-section, and at where the box goes after every polish.
challenges.why: 100 times, once per layer: deposit, print, etch, clean, polish, measure, then round again. The first quarter of the layers also go through implant and anneal to make the transistors. That is why one scarce machine touches everything. A leading-edge chip takes 1,000 or more process steps.

challenges.title: Full is slow
challenges.task: With the phone chip and the fab as you found it, start at 70% full and push the starts up to 95%. What happens to the time each chip takes?
challenges.hint: Watch the stockers fill and the dot climb the curve.
challenges.why: Output rises by about a third, but each phone chip takes about two and a half times as long: from about 63 to 154 days. Near full, boxes queue at every bay. This is why a shortage cannot be fixed by running fabs harder, and why real fabs run below 100%.

challenges.title: Buy one machine
challenges.task: Reset the fab, then add exactly one machine to make phone chips. Which one raises the most wafers a day the fab can make?
challenges.hint: The red row is the busiest group.
challenges.why: Only a scanner helps, by about 14%, and the moment you add it, deposition becomes the bottleneck. Any other machine changes nothing at all. A fab is only as fast as its busiest group of machines.

challenges.title: Double the output
challenges.task: Make twice as many phone-chip wafers a day as the starting fab can (19.8 a day) while changing as few machines as you can. Can you do it with 16?
challenges.hint: Add a machine to whichever row is red, and keep going until the most it can make reaches 19.8.
challenges.why: It takes 16 more machines, in every bay: 3 scanners, 4 deposition, 2 etch, 2 clean, 1 implanter, 1 furnace, 2 polishers, 1 inspection tool. Doubling output means nearly doubling the fab, not just the famous machine, which is why new capacity takes years and billions. One surprise: at the same share of full, each chip goes a little faster, because bigger groups of machines absorb bumps better.

challenges.title: What EUV really saves
challenges.task: Keep the phone chip and its starts, then switch printing to 193 nm light with two patterns. What gets worse, and why?
challenges.hint: Watch which row turns red, and the count of machine visits.
challenges.why: The older scanners are not slower, but every fine layer now needs a second pattern: deposit, print and etch again. A phone chip goes from 520 to 592 machine visits, deposition becomes the bottleneck, and at the same starts each chip takes about 239 days instead of 87. EUV's real gift is fewer steps.

challenges.title: One company, every chip
challenges.task: Stop ASML's shipments, then try to double the fab's output.
challenges.hint: The stop button is on the Scanners card. Then add machines where the fab needs them most.
challenges.why: You cannot. Without new scanners, the fab can never make more than its scanners allow, about 10 phone-chip wafers a day here, whatever else you buy. Every leading-edge fab depends on ASML for EUV, and ASML on Zeiss for mirrors and Trumpf for lasers.

challenges.title: Smarter, not bigger
challenges.task: Run the phone fab as you found it at 90% full, then switch AI on. How much faster does each chip come out?
challenges.hint: Set the starts in Measure it first, then come back to the AI card.
challenges.why: From about 106 to 85 days, a fifth faster, with exactly the same machines: smoother flow means shorter queues. The size of the effect here is illustrative, but the lesson is real: near full, surprises cost more than machines.

learn.plain: A chip factory is not an assembly line. A box of 25 wafers goes round the same machines once for every layer of the chip: put down a film, print a pattern in light, etch it, clean, polish, measure, and again, 45 to 100 times. Like a busy airport, the slowest gate sets the pace, and the fuller the factory, the longer each box waits in line. That waiting is most of the three months a chip spends inside.
learn.engineer: The model is a re-entrant flow line of eight tool groups. Utilization u = starts × visits × process time ÷ (tools × availability); the bottleneck is the group with the highest u, and it caps throughput. Queue time per visit follows the Kingman–Sakasegawa approximation, Wq ≈ (ca² + cs²)/2 · u^(√(2(m+1))−1)/(m(1−u)) · te, summed over every visit plus an hour per layer for moves; Little's law gives work in progress. Times are tuned so an 85%-loaded line takes about 1 to 1.5 days per layer, as ECIA reports. It leaves out tool failures and repairs, hot lots, product mix, rework and scrap.

quiz.q: A fab is 95% full and customers want chips sooner. What helps most?
options: Start even more wafers each day
Add machines to the busiest group, or start fewer wafers
Add machines to the least busy group
quiz.why: Near full, waiting grows steeply. Only the bottleneck limits output, and lowering how full it is shortens every queue; more starts make the wait longer still.

quiz.q: Why does a 100-layer chip take longer than a 45-layer one in the same fab?
options: Its box goes round the bays more than twice as many times
quiz.why: Each layer is another trip through deposition, lithography, etch, clean, polish and measure, with a queue at each one.

quiz.q: Without EUV, what slows a phone chip down most?
options: The older scanners are much slower
Fine layers need a second pattern, so more deposit, print and etch steps
quiz.why: Double patterning repeats deposit, print and etch on each fine layer. The extra visits, not slower scanners, push deposition past its limit.
